title: Why Do Humans Tell Stories?
paragraphs: Storytelling appears to be a human universal: anthropologists have yet to find a society without it. From ancient myths and folk tales to novels, films and video games, narrative remains one of the principal means by which people make sense of experience, transmit values and entertain one another.

For the greater part of human history, stories circulated orally. In the absence of writing, communities depended on storytellers to preserve collective memory, account for natural phenomena and model acceptable behaviour. Devices such as rhythm, repetition and formulaic phrasing were not merely decorative; they made long narratives memorable enough to survive across generations.

With the advent of writing, some of these traditions were committed to clay and parchment. The Epic of Gilgamesh, composed in ancient Mesopotamia, is widely regarded as one of the earliest surviving works of literature, and its preoccupation with friendship, mortality and the limits of human ambition continues to resonate with modern readers.

Several explanations have been proposed for the enduring power of narrative. Because stories bind events together through causation and emotion, the information they carry tends to be more memorable than isolated facts. They also require us to simulate the perspectives of others, and a number of studies have associated reading fiction with enhanced social understanding, though researchers continue to debate the strength and direction of that link.
